metadata.title: An Ogilvy Lens on Behavrix — Satwika
metadata.ogilvy_note: Food for thought — not a grade. Ogilvy is one lens among several, running alongside the course rubric. The maker decides.

beats.narration_text: Satwika's Behavrix pitch. Human Risk Intelligence Platform — eighty percent of breaches are caused by people, not firewalls, not software. AI analyzes 270 real attack records and delivers a vendor risk report in ninety seconds at a fraction of a cent. The product is live today. What would David Ogilvy ask about it?

props.command: I just watched Satwika's Behavrix pitch — Human Risk Intelligence Platform. 80% of breaches are caused by people, not firewalls. AI analyzes 270 real attack records, delivers a vendor risk report in 90 seconds at $0.002. Competitors charge $25K and take 6 weeks. The product is live today. What do David Ogilvy's principles say about how this pitch frames the work? Not a score. Just the questions a great ad man would ask.

beats.act: RECONSTRUCT — Slide 1: The Headline Is Already There
beats.role_note: Show Slide 1, rebuild. '80% of breaches caused by people' is already Ogilvy-quality. Push it one step further.
beats.narration_text: Slide 1 — the headline. Eighty percent of breaches are caused by people — not firewalls, not software. We make human behavioral risk visible. That statistic is already Ogilvy-quality: specific, sourced, unsettling. The tagline is strong. But visible is passive. Ogilvy would ask: what if the tagline made the number land harder? We show exactly how your people get breached. That is the same claim — active.

beats.act: LENS 1 — What Gets Breached in Six Weeks
beats.role_note: Show Slide 2 (problem), rebuild. 6 weeks for one vendor assessment — Ogilvy: what happens in those 6 weeks?
beats.narration_text: Slide 2 — the problem. Nine and a half trillion dollars in annual cybercrime. Twenty-five thousand dollars for one consulting engagement. Six weeks to get one vendor risk assessment. The comparison to Behavrix — ninety seconds, two thousandths of a cent — is the whole pitch. Ogilvy would stop here and ask: what gets breached in those six weeks? That is the line this slide is reaching for.

beats.act: LENS 2 — The Live Product on the Title Slide
beats.role_note: Show Slide 1 again — 'Try Behavrix Live' CTA is ON the title slide. Ogilvy: right call.
beats.narration_text: There is a live product button on the title slide. Try Behavrix Live. That is the right call. Ogilvy: the most powerful word is free — close behind it is now. Putting the live product call-to-action on Slide 1 means the audience could try it before the pitch ends. Most products bury the live demo on Slide 9. This one leads with it. The question worth sitting with: does the audience know they can click that button right now?

beats.role_note: Show Slide 3 (Behavrix vs Alternatives), rebuild. The specific price comparison is the whole competitive claim.
beats.narration_text: Slide 3 — Behavrix versus alternatives. AI delivers in ninety seconds for two thousandths of a cent. A consulting firm takes six weeks and charges twenty-five thousand dollars. That is not a price comparison — it is a category disruption claim stated as a number. Ogilvy: specifics in a competitive claim always outperform generalities. This one has three: the time, the price, and the headcount. This slide earns its place.

beats.act: LENS 4 — The Close Earns Its Question
beats.role_note: No slide needed. 'Are you in?' is a bold close — Ogilvy: does the pitch earn it?
beats.narration_text: The closing ask ends with: the human risk gap is real. The product is live. Are you in? That last line is brave. Ogilvy approved of directness in advertising — he believed it was the only honest approach. But directness in a close only lands when the pitch has built to it. The question is whether everything before that line has done the work. Statistics, live product, specific price — this pitch does the work. The question earns its place.

beats.role_note: Show Slide 10 (ask), rebuild. $150K seed, 15% equity, advisory board — specific and right-sized.
beats.narration_text: Slide 10 — the ask. One hundred fifty thousand dollars. Fifteen percent equity. Advisory board seat. Sixty thousand for engineering, forty for data, thirty for go-to-market, twenty for operations. Specific allocations, ninety-day milestones. Ogilvy: a close should give the reader everything they need to act. This one does. The final line — are you in — is a direct question. That is the correct way to close a pitch that has earned it.

beats.role_note: Not a verdict: four questions for the next draft.
beats.narration_text: Not a verdict — a lens set. Four questions for the next draft. One: 'we make human risk visible' is good — can the tagline be more active? Two: six weeks and twenty-five thousand dollars — what gets breached in that wait? Three: 'Try Behavrix Live' on Slide 1 is the right call — does the audience know they can click it? Four: 'are you in?' is brave — does the pitch build to earn it? These are Ogilvy's questions. The pitch decides which ones matter.
